## What this exercise is

Exercises 1--3 ran on data that shipped inside an R package. This one
does not. You will work with **real surveillance data** --- COVID-19
deaths in the 67 counties of Pennsylvania --- and assemble the analysis
dataset yourself, the way you would in a health department: a table of
counts from one source, county boundaries from another, and a join
between them that has to be checked rather than trusted.

From there the exercise follows the sequence of the last two weeks:

1.  join and project the data;
2.  compute crude rates, **expected counts**, and the **standardized
    mortality ratio (SMR)**;
3.  map the SMR honestly --- which, for a ratio, is not the same as
    mapping a rate;
4.  build a spatial weights matrix and ask, with **global Moran's I**,
    whether the SMRs are spatially structured or could plausibly be
    arranged at random.

It is worth 17.5 points and carries more weight than the first two
exercises. Start early: Part A is where most of the unexpected problems
will be.

## The data

**Counts.** `pa_covid_deaths_2020.csv` is posted on Course Site. It is a
subset of the **Johns Hopkins University CSSE COVID-19 Data Repository**
(`time_series_covid19_deaths_US.csv`), the source behind the JHU
dashboard that was the most widely used COVID-19 tracker in the United
States until the project stopped updating in March 2023. The repository
compiles counts reported by state health departments --- here, the
Pennsylvania Department of Health --- and attributes deaths to the
county of residence.

| Column | Meaning |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `UID`, `FIPS` | JHU identifier; county FIPS code |
| `Admin2` | County name |
| `Province_State` | State |
| `Population` | County population (U.S. Census Bureau 2019 estimate, as carried in the JHU file) |
| `deaths_2020` | Cumulative COVID-19 deaths reported through December 31, 2020 |

Cite the source in your document as: Dong, E., Du, H., & Gardner, L.
(2020). An interactive web-based dashboard to track COVID-19 in real
time. *The Lancet Infectious Diseases, 20*(5), 533--534, together with
the repository URL: <https://github.com/CSSEGISandData/COVID-19>.

**Boundaries.** County polygons come from the U.S. Census Bureau's
**cartographic boundary files**, downloaded inside your document with
the `tigris` package. Install it once, in the console ---
`install.packages(c("tigris", "ggrepel"))` --- not inside the document.

::: callout-note
## Why 2020

Calendar year 2020 is the first pandemic year and the period before
vaccines were available. Treat the population as the population at risk
for one year.
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(leaflet)
library(spdep)
library(ggrepel)            # non-overlapping labels
library(tigris)
options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)   # download once, then reuse

covid <- read_csv("data/pa_covid_deaths_2020.csv")
pa    <- counties(state = "PA", cb = TRUE, year = 2020)
```

## Part A --- Assemble the dataset (3 points)

1.  Inspect both objects. How many rows does `covid` have, and how many
    polygons does `pa` have? The two numbers differ. Find the rows
    responsible and say in one sentence what they are and why they
    cannot be mapped.
2.  Identify the column in each object that identifies a county. Show
    what the values look like in each, and say why they will not match
    as they stand.
3.  Create a join key in `covid` that matches the one in `pa`, then
    **join the counts onto the polygons**. Show, with code, that every
    one of the 67 counties received a count --- do not just look at the
    map.
4.  In two or three sentences: why join the table onto the polygons
    (`left_join(pa, covid)`) rather than the other way around, and what
    would an **inner** join have hidden from you if the key had been
    only partly wrong?

::: callout-tip
Run the obvious join first,
`left_join(pa, covid, by = c("GEOID" = "FIPS"))`, and read the error
message carefully. It tells you exactly what is wrong. A FIPS code is an
**identifier**, not a number: `42001` and `42001.0` are the same number
but not the same identifier, and a county such as `01001` in Alabama
would lose its leading zero.
:::

### Starting code

```{r}
#| label: a-solution

# A1 — Inspect both objects and compare their sizes.
covid
pa

nrow(covid)  # 69 rows
nrow(pa)     # 67 county features

# Identify reporting rows without a matching county polygon.
anti_join(
  covid,
  st_drop_geometry(pa),
  by = c("Admin2" = "NAME")
) |>
  select(Admin2, FIPS, Population, deaths_2020)

# Check for missing values in the surveillance table.
covid |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x))))


# A2 — Examine the county identifiers.
str(covid$FIPS)
str(pa$GEOID)

# Show example values and their types.
head(covid$FIPS)
head(pa$GEOID)

# Display the original join error without stopping the render.
tryCatch(
  left_join(pa, covid, by = c("GEOID" = "FIPS")),
  error = function(e) {
    cat("Original join error:\n", conditionMessage(e), "\n")
  }
)


# A3 — Create a five-character, zero-padded text key.
covid <- covid |>
  mutate(GEOID = sprintf("%05d", as.integer(FIPS)))

# Confirm that both datasets have complete, unique keys.
stopifnot(
  !anyNA(covid$GEOID),
  !anyNA(pa$GEOID),
  anyDuplicated(covid$GEOID) == 0L,
  anyDuplicated(pa$GEOID) == 0L
)

# Join the counts onto the polygons using GEOID.
pa_covid <- pa |>
  left_join(covid, by = "GEOID")

# Show that all 67 counties received a count.
pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarise(
    total_counties = n(),
    unique_counties = n_distinct(GEOID),
    counties_with_counts = sum(!is.na(deaths_2020)),
    missing_counts = sum(is.na(deaths_2020))
  )

sum(is.na(pa_covid$deaths_2020))  # Expected result: 0

# Stop if the joined dataset fails the required checks.
stopifnot(
  nrow(pa_covid) == 67L,
  n_distinct(pa_covid$GEOID) == 67L,
  !anyNA(pa_covid$deaths_2020),
  !anyNA(pa_covid$Population),
  all(pa_covid$Population > 0)
)
```

##Answer 1.The covid table has 69 rows, while pa has 67 counties. The
two extra rows, “Out of PA” and “Unassigned,” are reporting categories
without matching Pennsylvania county boundaries, so they cannot be
mapped as counties.

2.TCounties are identified by FIPS in covid and GEOID in pa. FIPS is
imported as a number, such as 42001, while GEOID is stored as text, such
as "42001". Converting FIPS to five-character text allows the keys to
match and preserves leading zeros where needed.

3.The counts are joined onto the polygons using GEOID. The verification
should return 67 total counties, 67 unique counties, 67 counties with
counts, and zero missing counts, demonstrating that every county
received a count.\
\
4.Joining the table onto the polygons preserves all 67 county features
and their geometry, making unmatched records visible as missing values.
Reversing the left join would preserve the surveillance table’s extra
reporting categories. An inner join would silently drop counties with
unmatched keys, hiding an incorrect join and leaving an incomplete
analysis dataset.

## Part B --- Coordinate reference system (1.5 points)

1.  What CRS do the Census boundaries arrive in? Geographic or
    projected?
2.  Transform `pa_covid` to a **projected** CRS appropriate for the
    whole state, and state its EPSG code. Pennsylvania is split between
    two State Plane zones (North and South) and two UTM zones, so the
    obvious choices each cover only part of the state --- say what you
    chose and why it is acceptable for a statewide map.
3.  One sentence: which of the operations in this exercise actually
    depend on the projection, and which do not?

### Starting code

```{r}
#| label: b-solution

# B1 — Inspect the original coordinate reference system.
st_crs(pa_covid)
st_crs(pa_covid)$epsg   # Expected: 4269 (NAD83)
st_is_longlat(pa_covid) # Expected: TRUE — geographic coordinates

# B2 — Transform to NAD83 / Conus Albers.
# This projected, equal-area CRS covers all of Pennsylvania.
pa_covid <- st_transform(pa_covid, crs = 5070)

# Verify the new CRS and coordinate units.
st_crs(pa_covid)$input
st_crs(pa_covid)$epsg        # 5070
st_crs(pa_covid)$units_gdal  # metre
st_is_longlat(pa_covid)     # FALSE — projected coordinates

# Confirm that the transformation preserved all county records.
stopifnot(
  st_crs(pa_covid)$epsg == 5070,
  !st_is_longlat(pa_covid),
  nrow(pa_covid) == 67L
)
```

##Answer 1.The Census county boundaries use NAD83 (EPSG:4269), a
geographic CRS that measures longitude and latitude in degrees. The
initial st_is_longlat() check returns TRUE.

2.I transformed pa_covid to NAD83 / Conus Albers (EPSG:5070), which uses
meters and preserves area. It covers all of Pennsylvania in one
coordinate system, avoiding the need to choose between the state’s
separate State Plane or UTM zones. This makes it suitable for statewide
county maps.

3.The projection affects the map’s appearance and where proportional
symbols are placed, while Leaflet needs a longitude–latitude copy in
EPSG:4326; joins, rates, expected deaths, SMRs, confidence intervals,
and Moran’s I remain unchanged when the neighbor relationships stay the
same..

## Part C --- Counts, rates, expected counts, and the SMR (4.5 points)

1.  Compute the **crude COVID-19 mortality rate per 100,000** for 2020
    in every county. Report the three highest and three lowest.
2.  Make two quick static maps with `ggplot2`, placed side by side: the
    **number of deaths** as **proportional symbols**, and the **crude
    rate** as a choropleth with a sequential, colour-blind-safe palette.
    Both need a legend title with units. In two or three sentences: why
    is a count shown with symbols rather than a choropleth, which
    counties stand out on each map, and why do the two maps tell
    different stories?
3.  Compute the **statewide reference rate**
    $r = \sum_i O_i / \sum_i P_i$, and from it the **expected count** in
    each county, $E_i = r \times P_i$. Show that
    $\sum_i E_i = \sum_i O_i$ and explain in one sentence why this must
    be so.
4.  Compute the **SMR**, $O_i / E_i$.
    a.  Interpret the SMR of one county of your choice in a full
        sentence a county commissioner could understand.
    b.  Divide each county's crude rate by the statewide rate and
        compare with the SMR. Explain why they are identical here, and
        what $E_i$ would have to take into account for the two to
        differ. *(This is where we are going later in the semester.)*
5.  Compute an exact **95% confidence interval** for every SMR (formula
    below). Compare the intervals for the two or three counties with the
    **fewest** deaths with those of the counties with the **highest**
    SMRs. In three or four sentences: what does this tell you about the
    extreme values on an SMR map?

::: callout-note
## Where the confidence interval comes from

Treat the expected count $E$ as a fixed constant and the observed count
as Poisson, $O \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu)$ with
$\mu = \text{SMR} \times E$. We first find an exact 95% interval for
$\mu$ and then divide both ends by $E$.

The lower bound $\mu_L$ is the value of $\mu$ at which observing $O$
**or more** deaths has probability 0.025; the upper bound $\mu_U$ is the
value at which observing $O$ **or fewer** has probability 0.025. Because
of the link between the Poisson and chi-square distributions, both have
a closed form:

$$\mu_L = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\chi^2_{0.025,\;2O}, \qquad
\mu_U = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\chi^2_{0.975,\;2(O+1)} .$$

Dividing by $E$ gives the interval for the SMR:

$$\left[\ \frac{\chi^2_{0.025,\,2O}}{2E}\ ,\ \ \frac{\chi^2_{0.975,\,2(O+1)}}{2E}\ \right].$$

The upper bound uses $2(O+1)$ degrees of freedom and the lower bound
$2O$; that asymmetry is what keeps the interval exact when counts are
small. When $O = 0$ the lower bound is 0.

**Worked example.** A county with $O = 4$ and $E = 5.57$ has SMR
$= 0.72$ and

``` r
qchisq(0.025, 2 * 4)       / (2 * 5.57)   # 0.20
qchisq(0.975, 2 * (4 + 1)) / (2 * 5.57)   # 1.84
poisson.test(4, T = 5.57)$conf.int        # same interval: E acts as the "time base"
```

The familiar normal approximation,
$\text{SMR} \times \exp(\pm 1.96/\sqrt{O})$, works for counties with
many deaths but breaks down for the smallest ones --- which are exactly
the counties this question is about --- and is undefined when $O = 0$.
:::

### Starting code

```{r}
#| label: c-solution
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Check required data before calculating rates.
stopifnot(
  nrow(pa_covid) == 67L,
  !anyNA(pa_covid$deaths_2020),
  !anyNA(pa_covid$Population),
  all(pa_covid$Population > 0),
  all(pa_covid$deaths_2020 >= 0),
  !st_is_longlat(pa_covid)
)


# C1 — Calculate crude mortality rates per 100,000.
pa_covid <- pa_covid |>
  mutate(crude_rate = 100000 * deaths_2020 / Population)

# Report the three highest rates.
pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(desc(crude_rate)) |>
  select(NAME, deaths_2020, Population, crude_rate) |>
  slice_head(n = 3)

# Report the three lowest rates.
pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(crude_rate) |>
  select(NAME, deaths_2020, Population, crude_rate) |>
  slice_head(n = 3)


# C2 — Map counts as proportional symbols and rates as a choropleth.

# Locate one point inside each county using the projected geometry.
pts <- st_point_on_surface(pa_covid)

p_count <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    data = pa_covid,
    fill = "grey95", colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.15
  ) +
  geom_sf(
    data = pts, aes(size = deaths_2020),
    shape = 21, fill = "firebrick", colour = "white", alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  # Symbol area, rather than radius, is proportional to deaths.
  scale_size_area(max_size = 14, name = "Deaths\n(number)") +
  labs(title = "COVID-19 deaths, 2020") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p_rate <- ggplot(pa_covid) +
  geom_sf(
    aes(fill = crude_rate),
    colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "magma", direction = -1,
    name = "Deaths per\n100,000 people"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Crude COVID-19 mortality rate, 2020") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

# Display the two maps side by side.
p_count + p_rate


# C3 — Calculate the statewide reference rate and expected deaths.

# r is deaths per person; multiply by 100,000 for reporting.
r <- sum(pa_covid$deaths_2020) / sum(pa_covid$Population)

tibble(
  total_deaths = sum(pa_covid$deaths_2020),
  total_population = sum(pa_covid$Population),
  statewide_rate_per_100000 = r * 100000
)

pa_covid <- pa_covid |>
  mutate(E = r * Population)

# Compare total expected and observed deaths.
tibble(
  total_expected = sum(pa_covid$E),
  total_observed = sum(pa_covid$deaths_2020)
)

# Allow for small floating-point differences.
stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    sum(pa_covid$E),
    as.numeric(sum(pa_covid$deaths_2020))
  ))
)


# C4 — Calculate SMRs and compare them with crude-rate ratios.
pa_covid <- pa_covid |>
  mutate(
    SMR = deaths_2020 / E,
    rate_ratio = crude_rate / (r * 100000)
  )

# Display one county for interpretation.
pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(NAME == "Mifflin") |>
  select(NAME, deaths_2020, E, SMR)

# Compare the two measures across all counties.
tibble(
  maximum_absolute_difference =
    max(abs(pa_covid$SMR - pa_covid$rate_ratio)),
  identical_within_numerical_tolerance =
    isTRUE(all.equal(pa_covid$SMR, pa_covid$rate_ratio))
)


# C5 — Calculate exact Poisson 95% confidence intervals.
pa_covid <- pa_covid |>
  mutate(
    # Explicitly set the lower bound to zero when no deaths occurred.
    SMR_lo = if_else(
      deaths_2020 == 0,
      0,
      qchisq(0.025, df = 2 * deaths_2020) / (2 * E)
    ),
    SMR_hi =
      qchisq(0.975, df = 2 * (deaths_2020 + 1)) / (2 * E)
  )

# Intervals for the three counties with the fewest deaths.
pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(deaths_2020, NAME) |>
  select(NAME, deaths_2020, E, SMR, SMR_lo, SMR_hi) |>
  slice_head(n = 3)

# Intervals for the three counties with the highest SMRs.
pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(desc(SMR)) |>
  select(NAME, deaths_2020, E, SMR, SMR_lo, SMR_hi) |>
  slice_head(n = 3)
```

##Answer 1. The three highest crude COVID-19 mortality rates were in
Mifflin County, at 257.92 deaths per 100,000 people, Northumberland
County, at 248.78 and Bedford County, at 196.29. The three lowest were
in Wayne County, at 35.05; Forest County, at 41.40; and Greene County,
at 41.40.

2.Proportional symbols show total deaths without allowing a county’s
geographic area to dominate the display. Philadelphia, Montgomery, and
Allegheny stand out for their large death counts, while Mifflin,
Northumberland, and Bedford have the highest mortality rates. The maps
tell different stories because counts show the total mortality burden,
whereas rates account for differences in population size.

3.  Pennsylvania recorded 16,030 deaths among 12,801,989 people, giving
    a statewide rate of 125.21 deaths per 100,000 people. Each county’s
    expected deaths were calculated by multiplying its population by the
    statewide rate per person. Expected deaths sum to 16,030 because
    applying this rate to the total population reproduces the statewide
    death total.

4a. Mifflin County recorded 119 deaths compared with approximately 57.77
expected if it had experienced the statewide mortality rate, so its SMR
of 2.06 indicates about 106% more deaths than expected

4b. The crude-rate ratio and SMR are identical because both compare the
county’s mortality rate with the same statewide rate. They could differ
if expected deaths also accounted for population characteristics, such
as each county’s age distribution. The SMRs calculated here account for
population size but are not age-adjusted

5\. Forest, Sullivan, and Cameron recorded only three, three, and four
deaths, respectively, and their SMR confidence intervals were 0.07–0.97,
0.08–1.15, and 0.20–1.84, indicating substantial uncertainty relative to
their estimates. Sullivan’s and Cameron’s intervals include 1, while
Forest’s upper bound is just below 1. Mifflin, Northumberland, and
Bedford had the highest SMRs, with relatively narrower intervals of
1.71–2.46, 1.74–2.26, and 1.27–1.92, all above 1 and supporting elevated
mortality under the assumed Poisson model. Extreme map colors should
therefore be interpreted alongside death counts and confidence
intervals, because estimates based on very few deaths can be unstable.

## Part D --- Mapping a ratio (3.5 points)

In Exercise 1 a sequential palette was the right choice for a rate. An
SMR is different: it is a ratio with a **meaningful reference value of
1**, and it is **multiplicative** --- an SMR of 2 is as far above
expected as 0.5 is below it.

1.  Map the SMR as an interactive **`leaflet`** map with a **diverging
    palette centred on 1** and **class breaks you set yourself**. Choose
    breaks that are symmetric on the ratio scale, and make the class
    around 1 read as "about as expected". Justify the palette and the
    breaks in three or four sentences.
2.  Your SMR map meets the standards from Exercise 1 --- legend title
    with units or meaning, thin boundaries, colour-blind-safe palette
    --- and in addition:
    - a **source line** on the map naming the data and the year;
    - a **popup** for each county giving the observed and expected
      deaths, the SMR, and its 95% interval from C5. This is what makes
      an interactive map worth having: the reader can check how much
      evidence stands behind a colour.

::: callout-warning
## `leaflet` wants longitude and latitude

Web maps are drawn on a Web Mercator basemap and expect coordinates in
**EPSG:4326**. Your `pa_covid` is now projected (Part B), so give
`leaflet` a transformed **copy**, `st_transform(pa_covid, 4326)`, and
keep the projected object for everything else. Handing it projected
coordinates is the most common reason for a blank `leaflet` map.
:::

::: callout-tip
## What earns full marks here

Breaks that follow from what an SMR *means*, not from the distribution
of the values. A student who can explain why 0.67 and 1.5 belong in the
same break set understands the variable.
:::

### Starting code

```{r}
#| label: d-solution

library(sf)
library(leaflet)

# Check that the SMRs and confidence intervals from Part C are complete.
stopifnot(
  !anyNA(pa_covid$SMR),
  !anyNA(pa_covid$E),
  !anyNA(pa_covid$SMR_lo),
  !anyNA(pa_covid$SMR_hi),
  all(is.finite(pa_covid$SMR)),
  all(pa_covid$SMR >= 0)
)

# Create a longitude-latitude copy for Leaflet.
# Keep pa_covid in its projected CRS for subsequent analysis.
pa_wgs <- st_transform(pa_covid, crs = 4326)


# D1 — Define classes symmetric on the multiplicative ratio scale.
# Reciprocal pairs: 0.5 and 2; 2/3 and 1.5; 0.8 and 1.25.
brks <- c(0, 0.5, 2/3, 0.8, 1.25, 1.5, 2, Inf)

# Seven colors from the diverging RdBu palette:
# blue = below expected; neutral = near 1; red = above expected.
smr_colors <- c(
  "#2166AC", "#67A9CF", "#D1E5F0", "#F7F7F7",
  "#FDDBC7", "#EF8A62", "#B2182B"
)

pal <- colorBin(
  palette = smr_colors,
  domain = pa_wgs$SMR,
  bins = brks,
  pretty = FALSE,
  right = FALSE
)

# Use explicit labels to explain the central class.
legend_labels <- c(
  "0 to <0.50",
  "0.50 to <0.67",
  "0.67 to <0.80",
  "0.80 to <1.25 (about as expected)",
  "1.25 to <1.50",
  "1.50 to <2.00",
  "2.00 or more"
)


# D2 — Build the interactive map with popups and source information.
leaflet(pa_wgs) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~pal(SMR),
    fillOpacity = 0.8,
    color = "white",
    weight = 0.6,
    label = ~NAME,
    popup = ~sprintf(
      paste0(
        "<b>%s County</b><br>",
        "Observed deaths: %.0f<br>",
        "Expected deaths: %.2f<br>",
        "SMR: %.2f<br>",
        "Exact 95%% CI: %.2f–%.2f"
      ),
      NAME, deaths_2020, E, SMR, SMR_lo, SMR_hi
    ),
    highlightOptions = highlightOptions(
      weight = 2,
      color = "black",
      bringToFront = TRUE
    )
  ) |>
  addLegend(
    position = "bottomright",
    colors = smr_colors,
    labels = legend_labels,
    opacity = 0.8,
    title = "SMR (observed / expected)<br>1 = as expected"
  ) |>
  addControl(
    html = paste0(
      "<b>Pennsylvania COVID-19 mortality, 2020</b><br>",
      "Deaths: JHU CSSE, through December 31, 2020.<br>",
      "Population: 2019 Census estimates in JHU data.<br>",
      "Boundaries: U.S. Census Bureau, 2020."
    ),
    position = "bottomleft"
  )
```

##Answer 1. I used a color-blind-safe blue–red palette, with blue
showing fewer deaths than expected, red showing more, and a light
neutral color around an SMR of 1. The breaks use matching pairs such as
0.5 and 2, because half the expected deaths and twice the expected
deaths represent equal changes in opposite directions. The other
matching pairs are approximately 0.67 and 1.5, and 0.8 and 1.25. The
central class, from 0.8 to below 1.25, is labeled “about as expected,”
although its color alone does not indicate statistical significance.

2.The map uses thin county boundaries and a legend explaining that the
SMR compares observed deaths with expected deaths. The source line
identifies the death data, population estimates, and county boundaries
with their years. Clicking a county displays its observed and expected
deaths, SMR, and exact 95% confidence interval, helping readers assess
the uncertainty behind its color.

::: callout-note
A `leaflet` map is an HTML widget: it appears in the rendered page on
your GitHub Pages site, which is where I grade it. It will not appear in
a PDF.
:::

## Part E --- Spatial weights and global Moran's I (4 points)

1.  Build a **queen contiguity** neighbour list. Report the average
    number of neighbours, the smallest and largest, and whether any
    county has none.
2.  Convert it to **row-standardized** spatial weights. One sentence:
    what does row standardization do to a county's neighbours, and what
    does the spatial lag of the SMR then represent?
3.  Compute **global Moran's I** for the SMR by permutation with
    `moran.mc()` (999 simulations; set a seed), and plot the permutation
    distribution with the observed value marked. Report $I$, its
    expectation under the null hypothesis, $-1/(n-1)$, and the
    $p$-value. In three or four sentences: what exactly is the null
    hypothesis, how does the simulation test it, and is there a spatial
    signal in the SMRs?
4.  Draw the **Moran scatterplot**, with every county labelled and
    coloured by quadrant. Name two or three counties in the high--high
    quadrant and two or three in the low--low quadrant, say in one
    sentence what the slope of the fitted line is, and say in one
    sentence what Moran's I does **not** tell you about these counties.

### Starting code

```{r}
#| label: e-solution
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 9

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(spdep)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)

# Check that all 67 counties have finite SMRs and projected coordinates.
stopifnot(
  nrow(pa_covid) == 67L,
  all(is.finite(pa_covid$SMR)),
  !st_is_longlat(pa_covid)
)


# E1 — Build queen-contiguity neighbors.
# Counties are neighbors if they share a boundary or corner.
nb <- poly2nb(
  pa_covid,
  queen = TRUE,
  row.names = pa_covid$GEOID
)

summary(nb)

# Count each county's neighbors.
n_neighbors <- card(nb)

cat(
  "Average neighbors:", round(mean(n_neighbors), 2),
  "\nSmallest number:", min(n_neighbors),
  "\nLargest number:", max(n_neighbors),
  "\nCounties with no neighbors:", sum(n_neighbors == 0),
  "\n"
)

# Require neighbors for every county before proceeding.
stopifnot(all(n_neighbors > 0))


# E2 — Create row-standardized spatial weights.
# Each neighbor receives weight 1 / number of neighbors.
lw <- nb2listw(nb, style = "W", zero.policy = FALSE)

# Verify that each county's neighbor weights sum to 1.
stopifnot(
  all(abs(vapply(lw$weights, sum, numeric(1)) - 1) < 1e-12)
)


# E3 — Run the permutation test for positive spatial autocorrelation.
set.seed(374)

mc <- moran.mc(
  pa_covid$SMR,
  listw = lw,
  nsim = 999,
  alternative = "greater",
  zero.policy = FALSE
)

mc

observed_I <- as.numeric(mc$statistic)
expected_I <- -1 / (nrow(pa_covid) - 1)
permutation_p <- mc$p.value

cat(
  "Observed Moran's I:", round(observed_I, 4),
  "\nExpected I under the null:", round(expected_I, 4),
  "\nPermutation p-value:", permutation_p,
  "\n"
)

# mc$res contains 999 simulated values followed by the observed value.
simulated_I <- mc$res[seq_len(999)]

hist(
  simulated_I,
  breaks = 40,
  xlim = range(c(simulated_I, observed_I)),
  main = "Permutation distribution of Moran's I",
  xlab = "Moran's I",
  col = "grey80",
  border = "white"
)

abline(v = observed_I, col = "#D55E00", lwd = 2)
abline(v = expected_I, col = "#0072B2", lwd = 2, lty = 2)

legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c("Observed I", "Expected I under the null"),
  col = c("#D55E00", "#0072B2"),
  lwd = 2,
  lty = c(1, 2),
  bty = "n"
)

# Save a conclusion for the written answer.
test_conclusion <- if (permutation_p < 0.05) {
  paste(
    "The result provides evidence of positive spatial autocorrelation:",
    "counties with similar SMRs tend to be neighbors."
  )
} else {
  paste(
    "The result does not provide sufficient evidence of positive spatial",
    "autocorrelation at the 5% significance level."
  )
}


# E4 — Calculate the spatial lag and assign scatterplot quadrants.
mean_SMR <- mean(pa_covid$SMR)

mp_df <- pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(
    lag_SMR = lag.listw(lw, SMR),
    quad = case_when(
      SMR >= mean_SMR & lag_SMR >= mean_SMR ~ "High-High",
      SMR < mean_SMR & lag_SMR < mean_SMR ~ "Low-Low",
      SMR >= mean_SMR & lag_SMR < mean_SMR ~ "High-Low",
      TRUE ~ "Low-High"
    )
  )

# Fit the same line shown in the scatterplot.
moran_fit <- lm(lag_SMR ~ SMR, data = mp_df)
moran_slope <- unname(coef(moran_fit)["SMR"])

# Save up to three examples from each requested quadrant.
hh_examples <- mp_df |>
  filter(quad == "High-High") |>
  arrange(NAME) |>
  slice_head(n = 3) |>
  pull(NAME)

ll_examples <- mp_df |>
  filter(quad == "Low-Low") |>
  arrange(NAME) |>
  slice_head(n = 3) |>
  pull(NAME)

cat(
  "High-High examples:", paste(hh_examples, collapse = ", "),
  "\nLow-Low examples:", paste(ll_examples, collapse = ", "),
  "\nFitted slope:", round(moran_slope, 4),
  "\n"
)

# Label every county and use distinct, color-blind-safe colors.
ggplot(mp_df, aes(x = SMR, y = lag_SMR)) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = mean_SMR,
    linetype = 2, colour = "grey60"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = mean_SMR,
    linetype = 2, colour = "grey60"
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm", formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = quad), size = 2.5) +
  geom_text_repel(
    aes(label = NAME),
    size = 2.6,
    max.overlaps = Inf,
    seed = 374
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "High-High" = "#D55E00",
      "Low-Low" = "#0072B2",
      "High-Low" = "#E69F00",
      "Low-High" = "#009E73"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Moran scatterplot of county SMRs",
    subtitle = "Dashed lines mark the mean county SMR",
    x = "County SMR (observed / expected deaths)",
    y = "Mean SMR of neighboring counties",
    colour = "Quadrant"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

##Answer 1. Using queen contiguity, counties are neighbors if they share
a boundary or corner. Each county has an average of 5.1 neighbors,
ranging from 2 to 9, and no county has zero neighbors.

2.Row standardization gives each county’s neighbors equal weights that
sum to 1, so the spatial lag represents the average SMR of its
neighboring counties.

3.The observed Moran’s I is 0.2893, compared with an expected value of
−0.0152 under the null hypothesis, with a permutation p-value of 0.001.
The null hypothesis is that SMRs are randomly arranged among counties,
with no relationship to the neighbor structure. The test shuffled the
SMRs among counties 999 times, and none of these arrangements produced a
Moran’s I as high as the observed value. This provides strong evidence
of positive spatial autocorrelation, meaning counties with similar SMRs
tend to be neighbors.

4.Bedford, Berks, and Blair are examples in the high–high quadrant,
meaning their SMRs and their neighbors’ average SMRs are above the mean
county SMR. Allegheny, Bradford, and Cameron are in the low–low
quadrant, meaning both values are below that mean. The fitted line has a
slope of 0.2893, equal to Moran’s I with these row-standardized weights.
Moran’s I describes the overall spatial pattern but does not show
whether these individual counties form statistically significant local
clusters or explain what caused the pattern.
